But indeed, it is even more marvelous that some people are found who not only inquire into this highest art <note>Ecclesiastes 7</note>, but even attempt to handle and practice it, and yet nevertheless doubt whether it is a natural or truly magical art, or instead a preternatural and necromantic art <note>necromancy: the forbidden practice of communicating with the dead or using demonic spirits</note> that is acquired only through illicit spirits and prohibited means. Not at all, my good man! Neither the Devil nor any of the impious have that power without divine permission, so that they might touch even the smallest part of this art, much less bring it under their own jurisdiction and practice it at their whim. Not in the least, I say; that art rests solely in the hand and power of God, who both imparts it to whom He wills and, at the same time, takes it away again. For to this art, which takes its origin from and out of God, no seekers of pleasure are admitted at all—much less the dire and infernal spirits—but rather, conversely, such a spirit as is simple, upright, true, constant, and of a pure and pious essence. Yet the modern world, in its careless impiety, does not recognize this spirit, and therefore remains ignorant of its essence and its highest mystery in many respects. For as soon as it hears anything of it with its ears, and yet is not able to comprehend it quickly, then these worldly companions <note>Wisdom of Solomon 1</note> call it foolishness. Therefore, because of their blindness, that spirit will be perpetually hidden from them and will finally be taken away from them altogether.

<note>A small ink flourish or doodle consisting of several wavy vertical and horizontal strokes appears in the right margin.</note>

Lest I proceed by this mention perhaps further than is right from my purpose, let me touch upon it again and finally lead it to a conclusion. Therefore, in place of a friendly exhortation, I wish this to be properly instilled in pious craftsmen: namely, to the extent that one directs his heart and mind—indeed, his life and actions—toward God <note>Ecclesiastes 18 and 29</note>, to that same extent he shall perceive a remarkable benefit in the progress of the stone and of his labor daily and even at every hour. This is what I myself have observed every day with the highest diligence and great devotion, and thus I have experienced it by the fact itself. For this reason, right from the beginning, one ought to direct all his actions toward this goal and prepare himself so that he may afterward be able to attain a more successful end in both works.
